about: Introduction to Aerospace (AERO40002) is a core, 5-credit Spring-term module in Year 1 of Imperial's MEng Aeronautical Engineering (H401). It surveys aerospace vehicles and their missions, then introduces the tools for analysing them: the standard atmosphere, aircraft components and controls, propulsion, lift and drag, the equations of motion, fixed-wing and rotorcraft performance, and static stability and trim. The topic order follows the department's module descriptor as recorded when this pack was written; Imperial's public pages checked here confirm only the title, status, term and credits and give no assessment breakdown, so check details on the module page.

notes.h: Aerospace vehicles and the missions that shape them
notes.body:
Introduction to Aerospace surveys the range of flying vehicles before the module turns to the numbers behind their performance. The central idea is that the mission (what the vehicle must carry, how far, how fast and from where) drives the design.

Main classes of vehicle
- Fixed-wing aircraft: lift from a wing moving forward through the air; thrust from propellers, turbofans or turbojets. Includes airliners, business jets, general aviation, military combat and transport aircraft, gliders and many uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs).
- Rotorcraft: lift from rotating wings (rotor blades), so they can hover and take off vertically. Helicopters (powered main rotor), autogyros (unpowered rotor that autorotates, with a separate propeller for thrust) and tiltrotors (rotors that tilt from vertical to forward flight).
- Lighter-than-air vehicles: balloons and airships, supported by buoyancy rather than aerodynamic lift.
- Launch vehicles and spacecraft: rockets carry their own oxidiser so they can work outside the atmosphere; spacecraft operate in orbit or beyond.

Speed regimes (by freestream Mach number, approximate boundaries)
- Subsonic: M below about 0.8.
- Transonic: about 0.8 to 1.2, where regions of local supersonic flow and shock waves appear.
- Supersonic: about 1.2 to 5.
- Hypersonic: above about 5, where high temperatures and thin shock layers dominate.
Most airliners cruise at roughly M 0.78–0.85, in the high subsonic range.

Missions and design drivers
- Transport: payload-range is the key measure. Long range rewards high lift-to-drag ratio, efficient engines and a high fuel fraction.
- Combat: manoeuvrability (high load factors), speed and sometimes stealth.
- Surveillance UAVs and gliders: endurance, so high aspect-ratio wings and low power required.
- Vertical take-off and landing: hover capability, so rotorcraft or powered-lift designs, at the cost of lower cruise efficiency.
- Space access: very high velocity. Low Earth orbit at 400 km needs about 7.7 km/s (from v = √(μ/r) with μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and r = 6771 km), and Earth escape from the surface needs about 11.2 km/s.

Trade-offs
Every choice has costs: a bigger wing lowers stall speed but adds weight and drag; more fuel extends range but cuts payload at a given take-off weight; hover ability costs cruise efficiency. Being able to state these trade-offs clearly is part of what the module expects.

Exam tips: give a mission requirement, then link it to a specific design feature and its penalty, and use approximate numbers to show scale.

notes.h: The International Standard Atmosphere and airspeeds
notes.body:
Aircraft performance depends on the air the vehicle flies through. The International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) defines a reference variation of temperature, pressure and density with altitude so that performance figures can be compared and instruments calibrated.

ISA basics
- Sea level: T₀ = 288.15 K, p₀ = 101 325 Pa, ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³, a₀ ≈ 340.3 m/s.
- Troposphere (0–11 km): T falls by 6.5 K per km.
- 11–20 km: constant temperature 216.65 K.
- The air is treated as a perfect gas (p = ρRT, R = 287.05 J/(kg K)) in hydrostatic equilibrium (dp/dh = −ρg).

Resulting formulae
- Troposphere: p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^5.256 and ρ/ρ₀ = (T/T₀)^4.256.
- Isothermal layer: p = p₁₁ exp[−g(h − 11 000)/(RT₁₁)], with p₁₁ ≈ 22.6 kPa.

Values worth remembering (approximate)
- 2 km: T ≈ 275 K, ρ ≈ 1.007 kg/m³ (σ ≈ 0.82).
- 10 km: T ≈ 223 K, p ≈ 26.4 kPa, ρ ≈ 0.413 kg/m³ (σ ≈ 0.34), a ≈ 300 m/s.
- 11 km: T = 216.65 K, ρ ≈ 0.364 kg/m³, a ≈ 295 m/s.

Altitudes
- Pressure altitude: ISA altitude with the same pressure as the actual air (what the altimeter reads when set to 1013.25 hPa). Flight levels are pressure altitudes in hundreds of feet.
- Density altitude: ISA altitude with the same density. On hot days it is above the actual altitude, so engines and wings perform as if the aircraft were higher.

Airspeeds
Aerodynamic forces depend on dynamic pressure q = ½ρV². Several "airspeeds" exist because the density changes:
- True airspeed (TAS): actual speed relative to the air.
- Equivalent airspeed (EAS): the sea-level speed that gives the same dynamic pressure, EAS = TAS × √σ.
- Indicated and calibrated airspeed (IAS, CAS): what the instrument shows, before and after correcting for instrument and position errors. At low speeds CAS ≈ EAS; compressibility makes them differ at high speed and altitude.
- Mach number: M = TAS/a.

Worked example: an aircraft flies at TAS 200 m/s at 10 km.
- σ = 0.413/1.225 ≈ 0.337, so EAS = 200 × √0.337 ≈ 116 m/s.
- a ≈ 299.5 m/s, so M ≈ 0.67.
Stall happens at a fixed EAS (for a given weight and CLmax), so the TAS at stall rises with altitude.

Exam tips: always work in kelvin, state σ, and say which airspeed you are using.

This part of the module introduces the main parts of an aircraft and the surfaces used to control it.

Major components
- Fuselage: carries the payload, crew and systems; in airliners it is a pressurised shell.
- Wing: produces lift and usually holds fuel; carries large bending loads to the fuselage.
- Empennage (tail): horizontal stabiliser (tailplane) and vertical stabiliser (fin), which provide stability and carry the elevator and rudder.
- Engines with nacelles and pylons; undercarriage (landing gear).

Semi-monocoque construction
Most aircraft structures combine a thin skin with internal stiffening members:
- Spars: run spanwise; spar caps (flanges) carry most of the bending, and spar webs carry shear.
- Ribs: run chordwise; keep the aerofoil shape and pass loads between skin and spars.
- Stringers: spanwise stiffeners that stop the thin skin buckling under compression.
- Skin: carries shear and, together with the spars, forms a closed box (the wing box) that resists torsion.
- The fuselage uses frames (rings) and longerons/stringers in the same way.

Axes and motions
- Roll: about the longitudinal (x) axis.
- Pitch: about the lateral (y) axis.
- Yaw: about the normal (z) axis.

Primary control surfaces
- Ailerons (outer trailing edge of the wings, deflect differentially): roll.
- Elevator (on the tailplane) or all-moving tailplane: pitch.
- Rudder (on the fin): yaw.
- Combined surfaces: elevons (elevator plus aileron, on tailless deltas) and ruddervators (V-tails).

Secondary surfaces
- Trailing-edge flaps: increase camber (and with Fowler flaps, wing area) to raise CLmax and lower stall speed, at the cost of more drag.
- Leading-edge slats: delay leading-edge stall so the wing can reach a higher angle of attack.
- Spoilers: raise on the upper surface to reduce lift and add drag (lift dumping after touchdown, speed brakes, roll assistance).
- Trim tabs: small surfaces that reduce or remove the control force the pilot must hold.

Adverse yaw
When the ailerons roll the aircraft, the down-going aileron on the rising wing raises that wing's lift and so its induced drag. The nose yaws away from the turn. Fixes include coordinated rudder, differential aileron deflection, Frise ailerons and roll spoilers.

Load factor
n = L/W. In steady level flight n = 1. Structures are designed to a limit load factor (for example +2.5 for large transport aircraft under certification rules, approximately) with an additional safety factor of 1.5 to give the ultimate load.

Exam tips: link each control surface to its axis, and each structural member to the load it mainly carries.

An aircraft in flight is acted on by four forces: lift, weight, thrust and drag. This topic covers how thrust is produced and how lift and drag are modelled for performance calculations.

Thrust from momentum
A propulsion system accelerates a mass of air (or exhaust) rearwards. For an air-breathing engine with exhaust at ambient pressure and ignoring fuel mass:
T = ṁ(Vₑ − V₀)
where V₀ is the flight speed and Vₑ the jet speed.

Propulsive (Froude) efficiency
ηₚ = useful power/power added to the stream = 2/(1 + Vₑ/V₀).
Efficiency is high when the jet is only slightly faster than the aircraft. So for a given thrust it is more efficient to accelerate a large mass of air a little than a small mass a lot.
Example: ṁ = 100 kg/s, V₀ = 250 m/s, Vₑ = 400 m/s gives T = 15 kN and ηₚ = 2/(1 + 1.6) ≈ 0.77.

Engine types
- Piston engine with propeller: efficient at low speed; general aviation.
- Turboprop: gas turbine driving a propeller; efficient up to roughly M 0.6–0.7.
- Turbojet: all air through the core; high jet velocity, so low propulsive efficiency at subsonic speeds.
- Turbofan: a large fan drives bypass air round the core. Bypass ratio = bypass mass flow/core mass flow. High bypass ratios (around 10 or more on recent airliner engines, approximately) give high propulsive efficiency and lower noise.
- Rocket: carries oxidiser. Ideal velocity change Δv = I_sp g₀ ln(m₀/m_f) (Tsiolkovsky). With I_sp = 300 s and a mass ratio of 5, Δv ≈ 4.7 km/s.

Lift
L = ½ρV²S CL. CL rises roughly linearly with angle of attack until near stall, then reaches CLmax.

Drag
- Parasite (zero-lift) drag: skin friction, form drag and interference drag, with coefficient CD₀.
- Induced (lift-dependent) drag: from the trailing vortex system, CDi = CL²/(πeAR).
- Wave drag at transonic and supersonic speeds.

The parabolic drag polar
CD = CD₀ + K CL², with K = 1/(πeAR).
- Minimum drag (maximum L/D) occurs where parasite and induced drag are equal: CD₀ = K CL².
- CL at (L/D)max = √(CD₀/K), and (L/D)max = 1/(2√(K CD₀)).

Worked example: CD₀ = 0.020, AR = 9, e = 0.8
- K = 1/(π × 0.8 × 9) ≈ 0.0442
- CL* = √(0.020/0.0442) ≈ 0.673
- (L/D)max = 1/(2√(0.0442 × 0.020)) ≈ 16.8

Drag in newtons: D = ½ρV²S CD₀ + K W²/(½ρV²S) in level flight, so parasite drag rises with V² and induced drag falls with 1/V².

Exam tips: state the assumptions behind T = ṁ(Vₑ − V₀); for drag-polar questions show the minimum-drag condition explicitly.

notes.h: Equations of motion for an aircraft
notes.body:
For performance work the aircraft is treated as a point mass moving in a vertical plane (or turning in a horizontal one). Resolving forces along and perpendicular to the flight path gives the equations used for climb, glide and turn.

Symmetric flight in the vertical plane
Let γ be the flight-path angle (positive in a climb) and assume thrust acts along the flight path.
- Along the path: T − D − W sin γ = m dV/dt
- Perpendicular to the path: L − W cos γ = m V dγ/dt

Steady level flight (γ = 0, constant V and γ):
L = W and T = D.

Steady climb
- With constant speed and γ: T − D = W sin γ and L = W cos γ (≈ W for shallow climbs).
- Climb angle: sin γ = (T − D)/W.
- Rate of climb: RC = V sin γ = (T − D)V/W = (power available − power required)/W, the specific excess power.
Example: m = 10 000 kg, T = 30 kN, D = 18 kN, V = 80 m/s. W = 98.1 kN, sin γ ≈ 0.122 (γ ≈ 7.0°), and RC ≈ 9.8 m/s.

Steady glide (T = 0)
- D = W sin γ and L = W cos γ, so tan γ = D/L = 1/(L/D).
- The flattest glide is at (L/D)max. With L/D = 15, the glide angle is about 3.8° and the aircraft covers about 15 km from 1000 m height in still air.

Level turn
With bank angle φ and no height change:
- Vertical: L cos φ = W.
- Horizontal: L sin φ = mV²/R.
Results:
- Load factor n = L/W = 1/cos φ.
- Turn radius R = V²/(g tan φ).
- Turn rate ω = V/R = g tan φ/V.
- Stall speed in the turn = V_s√n.
Example: V = 100 m/s, φ = 30°: n ≈ 1.155, R ≈ 1770 m, ω ≈ 0.057 rad/s (about 3.2° per second). At φ = 60°, n = 2 and the stall speed rises by a factor of √2 ≈ 1.41.

Pull-up
In a vertical pull-up at the bottom of a loop, L − W = mV²/R, so n = 1 + V²/(gR).

Exam tips: draw a free-body diagram with the flight path, resolve along and normal to it, and check whether the question assumes small angles (cos γ ≈ 1).

notes.h: Fixed-wing performance: stall, minimum drag, range and endurance
notes.body:
Performance analysis combines the drag polar with the equations of motion to predict speeds, range and endurance.

Stall speed
In level flight W = ½ρV²S CL, so the slowest steady speed is
V_s = √(2W/(ρS CLmax)).
Example: m = 60 000 kg, S = 120 m², CLmax = 2.4 with flaps, sea level: V_s = √(2 × 588 600/(1.225 × 120 × 2.4)) ≈ 57.8 m/s. With a clean-wing CLmax of 1.5 it would be about 73 m/s. Flaps and slats exist to cut this.

Drag and power required
- Level-flight drag D = ½ρV²S CD₀ + 2KW²/(ρV²S).
- Minimum drag speed: V_md = √(2W/(ρS)) × (K/CD₀)^(1/4), where CL = √(CD₀/K) and L/D is a maximum. Minimum drag D_min = W/(L/D)max.
- Power required P = DV. The minimum-power speed is V_mp = 3^(−1/4)V_md ≈ 0.76V_md (where the induced drag is three times the parasite drag).
- Below V_md, flying slower needs more thrust: the "back of the drag curve", where speed is unstable.

Best speeds (simple models)
- Jet (thrust roughly constant with speed, TSFC constant):
  - Maximum endurance at V_md (maximum L/D).
  - Maximum range at maximum √CL/CD, which is at 3^(1/4)V_md ≈ 1.32V_md.
- Propeller (power roughly constant, constant efficiency):
  - Maximum endurance at V_mp (maximum CL^(3/2)/CD).
  - Maximum range at V_md (maximum L/D).

Breguet range equation (jet, cruise at constant V and L/D)
R = (V/c)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁)
where c is the thrust-specific fuel consumption expressed as weight of fuel per unit thrust per unit time (units 1/s), W₀ is the start weight and W₁ the end weight.
Endurance for a jet: E = (1/c)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁).
For a propeller aircraft: R = (ηₚ/c_p)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁), with c_p as weight of fuel per unit power per unit time.

Worked example: V = 230 m/s, L/D = 17, c = 0.6 per hour = 1.667 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, fuel burnt 20% of the start weight (W₀/W₁ = 1.25).
R = (230/1.667 × 10⁻⁴) × 17 × ln 1.25 ≈ 5.2 × 10⁶ m, about 5200 km.

Take-off and landing
Ground roll depends strongly on the speed reached, which scales with V_s, so field length grows roughly with W/(ρS CLmax) divided by the average acceleration. Hot, high and heavy conditions all lengthen the take-off.

Exam tips: watch the units of fuel consumption (per hour versus per second, mass versus weight), and say whether you are optimising range or endurance for a jet or a propeller aircraft.

notes.h: Rotorcraft performance: hover and forward flight
notes.body:
Rotorcraft trade cruise efficiency for the ability to hover. Simple momentum theory gives the key hover results, and the asymmetry of the rotor in forward flight explains the speed limits.

Momentum (actuator disc) theory in hover
Model the rotor as a thin disc of area A = πR² that adds momentum to the air passing through it. Assume steady, incompressible, inviscid, uniform flow through the disc.
- Air arrives from rest far above, passes the disc at the induced velocity vᵢ, and reaches 2vᵢ in the far wake.
- Thrust = rate of change of momentum: T = ṁ(2vᵢ) with ṁ = ρAvᵢ, so T = 2ρAvᵢ².
- Hence vᵢ = √(T/(2ρA)).
- Ideal (induced) power: P = Tvᵢ = T^(3/2)/√(2ρA).

Key consequences
- Disc loading T/A: lower disc loading (bigger rotor) means smaller vᵢ and less power per unit thrust. This is why helicopters have large rotors.
- Power rises as density falls: P ∝ 1/√ρ, so hovering at altitude or on hot days needs more power.
- Figure of merit FM = ideal power/actual power. It accounts for profile drag of the blades, non-uniform inflow and tip losses. Typical good rotors have FM of roughly 0.7–0.8 (approximately).

Worked example: m = 5000 kg, R = 7.5 m, sea level
- T = 49 050 N, A = 176.7 m², disc loading ≈ 278 N/m²
- vᵢ = √(49 050/(2 × 1.225 × 176.7)) ≈ 10.6 m/s
- Ideal power ≈ 49 050 × 10.64 ≈ 522 kW
- With FM = 0.75, actual power ≈ 696 kW
- At 2000 m in the ISA (ρ ≈ 1.007 kg/m³), ideal power rises to about 576 kW, by the factor √(1.225/1.007) ≈ 1.10.

Controls
- Collective pitch changes the pitch of all blades together: more or less thrust.
- Cyclic pitch varies blade pitch once per revolution, tilting the rotor's thrust to move forwards, backwards or sideways.
- A tail rotor (or a second main rotor turning the other way) balances the torque reaction of the main rotor; otherwise the fuselage would spin.

Forward flight
- The advancing blade sees ΩR + V at its tip and the retreating blade ΩR − V. Without correction, lift would be unequal (dissymmetry of lift).
- Blades flap up on the advancing side and down on the retreating side, and cyclic pitch adjusts, which balances the rolling moment.
- Maximum speed is limited by retreating-blade stall (high angle of attack on the slow side) and compressibility on the advancing tip (approaching sonic speed), with a reverse-flow region near the retreating blade root.
- Power required first falls with forward speed (induced power drops as more air passes through the disc), then rises as parasite and profile power grow.

Autorotation
If the engine fails, lowering the collective lets air flow up through the descending rotor and keep it turning, so the pilot can glide down and flare to land.

Exam tips: derive T = 2ρAvᵢ² carefully using the far-wake velocity 2vᵢ, and always state the assumptions of momentum theory.

An aircraft must be able to fly steadily with no net moment (trim) and must tend to return towards that condition if disturbed (static stability). This topic introduces both ideas, mainly for pitch (longitudinal) motion.

Definitions
- Trim: equilibrium with zero resultant force and moment about the centre of gravity (CG). For pitch: Cm,cg = 0.
- Static stability: the initial tendency after a disturbance. Statically stable means the disturbance creates a moment that opposes it.
- Dynamic stability: how the motion develops over time (whether oscillations die away). An aircraft can be statically stable but dynamically unstable.

Longitudinal static stability
Write the pitching moment about the CG as Cm = Cm₀ + Cm_α α, where α is measured from zero lift.
- Stability needs Cm_α < 0: a nose-up gust (α rises) produces a nose-down moment.
- Trim at a useful positive lift needs Cm₀ > 0. A conventional wing on its own usually has Cm₀ < 0, so a tailplane (or reflex camber, or sweep with twist on a flying wing) is used to give positive Cm₀.

The tailplane
- The tail sits behind the CG. If α increases, tail lift rises, producing a nose-down moment: the tail is stabilising.
- Tail volume coefficient V_H = l_t S_t/(S c̄), where l_t is the distance from CG to tail aerodynamic centre, S_t tail area, S wing area and c̄ mean aerodynamic chord. Typical airliner values are roughly 0.5–1 (approximately). Example: l_t = 12 m, S_t = 25 m², S = 120 m², c̄ = 4 m gives V_H = 0.625.

Neutral point and static margin
- The neutral point is the CG position at which Cm_α = 0 (neutral stability). Its position as a fraction of c̄ is h_n.
- Static margin Kₙ = h_n − h, where h is the CG position as a fraction of c̄.
- dCm/dCL = −Kₙ, so Cm_α = −a Kₙ, where a is the lift-curve slope.
- Moving the CG forward increases the static margin and stability; moving it aft reduces it. Aft of the neutral point the aircraft is unstable. Too far forward makes it hard to trim at low speed (not enough elevator authority).

Worked example
h_n = 0.45 and h = 0.30, so Kₙ = 0.15. With a = 5.0 per rad, Cm_α = −0.75 per rad. If Cm₀ = 0.05, trim is at α = 0.05/0.75 ≈ 0.067 rad (3.8°) and CL,trim = 5.0 × 0.067 ≈ 0.33. To trim at a different CL, the elevator changes Cm₀.

Lateral and directional stability
- Directional (weathercock) stability: the fin makes the aircraft yaw into a sideslip, so Cn_β > 0 with the usual sign convention.
- Lateral (roll) stability: dihedral, high wing position and sweep make the aircraft roll away from a sideslip, so Cl_β < 0.

Exam tips: state your sign convention, show both conditions (Cm_α < 0 and Cm₀ > 0), and define static margin relative to the mean aerodynamic chord.

cards.b: Fixed-wing aircraft get lift from a wing moving forward; rotorcraft get lift from rotating blades, which allows hover.
A rotorcraft whose rotor is unpowered and autorotates in the airflow; forward thrust comes from a separate propeller. It cannot hover.
Roughly M 0.8–1.2: mixed subsonic and supersonic flow around the vehicle, with shock waves and drag rise.
Roughly M > 5: very high temperatures, thin shock layers and strong heating effects.

The ISA altitude with the same density; high on hot days, which reduces engine and wing performance.

Maintain the aerofoil shape and transfer loads between skin, stringers and spars.
Spanwise stiffeners that increase the buckling resistance of thin skin panels.
Ailerons → roll (longitudinal axis); elevator → pitch (lateral axis); rudder → yaw (normal axis).
Yaw away from the intended turn caused by extra induced drag on the up-going wing (with its aileron down).
Flaps (trailing edge) add camber and sometimes area to raise CLmax; slats (leading edge) delay stall to higher α.
Upper-surface panels that reduce lift and add drag: lift dumping, speed braking and roll control.
n = L/W; equals 1 in steady level flight and 1/cos φ in a level turn at bank angle φ.

cards.f: How parasite and induced drag vary with speed (level flight)
cards.b: Parasite drag ∝ V²; induced drag ∝ 1/V². Total drag has a minimum at V_md.
T − D − W sin γ = m dV/dt (thrust along the flight path).

cards.f: Equation normal to the flight path
cards.b: L − W cos γ = m V dγ/dt.
RC = V sin γ = (T − D)V/W = excess power/weight.
tan γ = 1/(L/D); flattest glide at (L/D)max.

cards.f: Load factor in a level turn
cards.b: n = 1/cos φ.
R = V²/(g tan φ).
ω = g tan φ/V.
V_s,turn = V_s√n; e.g. a 60° bank (n = 2) raises stall speed by about 41%.
V_s = √(2W/(ρS CLmax)).
V_md = √(2W/(ρS))(K/CD₀)^(1/4); occurs at (L/D)max where CD₀ = K CL².
V_mp = 3^(−1/4)V_md ≈ 0.76V_md; induced drag is three times parasite drag there.
R = (V/c)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁), c = TSFC as fuel weight per thrust per time.

cards.f: Jet: best range vs best endurance speed
cards.b: Endurance at V_md (max L/D); range at ≈1.32V_md (max √CL/CD).

cards.f: Propeller: best range vs best endurance speed
cards.b: Range at V_md (max L/D); endurance at V_mp ≈ 0.76V_md (max CL^1.5/CD).
Speeds below V_md, where slowing down increases drag; speed is unstable without throttle correction.
vᵢ = √(T/(2ρA)) from actuator disc (momentum) theory.
2vᵢ: twice the induced velocity at the disc.
FM = ideal (momentum theory) power/actual power; roughly 0.7–0.8 for good rotors.
Collective changes all blade pitches together (thrust); cyclic varies pitch around the revolution (tilts thrust).
In forward flight the advancing blade sees higher airspeed than the retreating blade; flapping and cyclic pitch balance it.
On the slow (retreating) side blades need high angle of attack to keep lift and may stall; a key limit on top speed.
Unpowered descent in which upward airflow through the rotor keeps it spinning, allowing a controlled landing.
Steady flight with zero pitching moment about the centre of gravity: Cm,cg = 0.
Static: initial tendency to return after a disturbance. Dynamic: how the motion evolves over time (do oscillations decay?).

cards.f: Conditions for longitudinal static stability and trim
cards.b: Cm_α < 0 (stability) and Cm₀ > 0 (trim at positive lift).
The CG position at which Cm_α = 0; the aircraft is neutrally stable in pitch.
Kₙ = h_n − h (fractions of mean aerodynamic chord); dCm/dCL = −Kₙ. Positive for stability.
V_H = l_t S_t/(S c̄): measures the tail's power to produce pitching moment.
The fin yaws the nose into a sideslip; Cn_β > 0 in the usual convention.

cards.f: Effect of moving the CG aft
cards.b: Reduces static margin and stability; aft of the neutral point the aircraft becomes statically unstable.

questions.q: An airliner cruising at M 0.82 is operating in which speed regime?
questions.why: M 0.82 is below 1 but close to it, so the aircraft is high subsonic, near the transonic range where local supersonic pockets can form. Supersonic flight needs M above about 1.2 and hypersonic above about 5. The incompressible approximation is only reasonable below about M 0.3.

questions.q: Approximately what speed is needed for a circular orbit 400 km above the Earth's surface?
questions.why: v = √(μ/r) = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴/6.771 × 10⁶) ≈ 7.67 km/s. 11.2 km/s is the escape speed from the surface. About 31.6 km/s comes from using the 400 km altitude as r instead of the orbital radius measured from the Earth's centre (6371 + 400 km). 340 m/s is the sea-level speed of sound.

questions.q: Choose two different aerospace missions and, for each, explain one design feature it drives and the penalty that feature brings.
markScheme: Mission 1 identified with a relevant requirement (e.g. long-range transport needs high L/D)
Design feature and penalty for mission 1 (e.g. high aspect ratio wing; heavier, more bending)
Mission 2 identified (e.g. VTOL rescue)
Design feature and penalty for mission 2 (e.g. rotor for hover; lower cruise speed and efficiency)
questions.modelAnswer: A long-range airliner must carry a payload a long way cheaply, so it needs a high lift-to-drag ratio. That pushes designers towards a high aspect-ratio wing to reduce induced drag, but a long slender wing has larger bending moments at the root, so it needs a heavier structure. A search-and-rescue mission needs to hover and land in confined spaces, which favours a helicopter. The rotor allows vertical flight, but helicopters cruise slower than fixed-wing aircraft because of retreating-blade stall and advancing-tip compressibility, and they use more power per unit weight carried.

questions.q: An aircraft flies at TAS 200 m/s at 10 km in the ISA (σ ≈ 0.337). What is its equivalent airspeed?
questions.why: EAS = TAS√σ = 200 × √0.337 ≈ 116 m/s. About 67 m/s multiplies by σ instead of √σ. About 345 m/s divides by √σ, which converts EAS to TAS rather than the reverse. 200 m/s is the TAS itself, which ignores the lower density.

questions.q: On a hot day at a high-altitude airfield, how does the density altitude compare with the airfield's actual elevation, and what is the effect?
options: The same, because density altitude depends only on pressure
Higher, but this has no effect on performance
questions.why: Higher temperature lowers density, so the air matches the ISA density of a greater altitude; engines give less thrust and the wing needs a higher true speed for the same lift, so take-off is longer. Density altitude falls below the elevation on cold (or high-pressure) days, not on hot ones. Density depends on both pressure and temperature, so it is not the same as pressure altitude in general. The effect on performance is real and significant.

questions.q: Explain why an aircraft's stall speed is roughly constant in terms of equivalent airspeed but rises in terms of true airspeed as it climbs.
markScheme: Lift = ½ρV²SCL; stall at CLmax
For L = W, ½ρV²S CLmax is fixed so ½ρV² (dynamic pressure) at stall is fixed
EAS is defined by the same dynamic pressure at sea-level density, so EAS at stall is constant
TAS = EAS/√σ and σ falls with altitude, so TAS at stall rises
questions.modelAnswer: In level flight L = W = ½ρV²S CL, and stall occurs at CLmax. For a given weight, the dynamic pressure at stall, ½ρV², is therefore fixed. Equivalent airspeed is defined as the sea-level speed giving the same dynamic pressure, so the stall EAS does not change with altitude. True airspeed is TAS = EAS/√σ, and σ falls as the aircraft climbs, so the true airspeed at stall increases with altitude.

questions.q: Which control surface is mainly used to control the aircraft in pitch?
questions.why: The elevator on the tailplane changes the tail lift and so the pitching moment. Ailerons control roll about the longitudinal axis, and the rudder controls yaw. Spoilers mainly dump lift and add drag, and can assist roll, but are not the pitch control.

questions.q: In a semi-monocoque wing, which component mainly prevents the thin skin from buckling under compression?
questions.why: Stringers are spanwise stiffeners attached to the skin that break it into smaller panels and raise its buckling load. Ribs keep the aerofoil shape and help support stringers, but their main role is shape and load transfer. The spar web mainly carries shear. Fuel tanks are not structural stiffeners (in many wings the fuel sits inside the wing box itself).

questions.q: Explain what causes adverse yaw when an aircraft rolls into a turn, and give two ways designers or pilots reduce it.
markScheme: Down-going aileron on the rising wing increases lift and hence induced drag
Extra drag on the rising (outside) wing yaws the nose away from the turn
Remedy 1, e.g. coordinated rudder input
Remedy 2, e.g. differential ailerons, Frise ailerons or roll spoilers
questions.modelAnswer: To roll right, the left aileron goes down and the right one goes up. The left wing gains lift, and because induced drag rises with lift it also gains drag, while the right wing loses some. The extra drag on the left (rising) wing yaws the nose to the left, away from the turn: this is adverse yaw. Pilots counter it with coordinated rudder in the direction of the turn. Designers reduce it with differential ailerons (the up-going aileron moves further than the down-going one), Frise ailerons (whose leading edge projects below the wing when raised, adding drag on the down-going wing), or by using spoilers for roll, which add drag on the descending wing.

questions.q: Why do modern airliners use high-bypass turbofans rather than turbojets?
options: Bypass air adds fuel energy directly to the stream
Accelerating a large mass of air by a small amount gives higher propulsive efficiency
High bypass ratio increases the jet exit velocity
questions.why: Thrust is ṁ(Vₑ − V₀); for the same thrust a large ṁ with a small velocity increase gives ηₚ = 2/(1 + Vₑ/V₀) closer to 1, and less noise. Turbojets can operate at high altitude (Concorde's engines did). A high bypass ratio lowers the mean jet velocity rather than raising it. Bypass air is not burned with fuel; it is driven by the fan.

questions.q: An aircraft has CD₀ = 0.02 and K = 0.0442. What is its maximum lift-to-drag ratio?
questions.why: (L/D)max = 1/(2√(K CD₀)) = 1/(2√(0.000884)) ≈ 16.8. About 33.6 omits the factor of 2 in the denominator. About 0.67 is the lift coefficient at (L/D)max, √(CD₀/K), not the ratio itself. About 50 is 1/CD₀, which ignores induced drag.

questions.q: A turbofan takes in 100 kg/s of air at a flight speed of 250 m/s and exhausts it at 400 m/s. Find the thrust and the propulsive efficiency. State two assumptions, and explain how increasing the mass flow while lowering the exhaust speed (for the same thrust) would change the efficiency.
markScheme: Assumptions: fuel mass flow neglected, exhaust pressure equal to ambient (no pressure thrust)
Larger ṁ with smaller Vₑ − V₀ for the same thrust raises ηₚ towards 1
Reason: less kinetic energy wasted in the jet
questions.modelAnswer: T = ṁ(Vₑ − V₀) = 100 × (400 − 250) = 15 000 N = 15 kN. Propulsive efficiency is ηₚ = 2/(1 + Vₑ/V₀) = 2/(1 + 1.6) ≈ 0.77. This assumes the fuel mass flow is negligible compared with the air flow and that the exhaust leaves at ambient pressure, so there is no pressure thrust. If the same 15 kN were produced with more mass flow and a smaller velocity increase, Vₑ/V₀ would fall towards 1 and ηₚ would rise, because less kinetic energy is left behind in the jet. That is the reason for high-bypass engines.

questions.q: An aircraft makes a level turn at 100 m/s with 30° of bank. What is the turn radius (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
questions.why: R = V²/(g tan φ) = 10 000/(9.81 × 0.577) ≈ 1770 m. About 1020 m is V²/g, which leaves out the bank angle altogether. About 2040 m uses sin 30° = 0.5 instead of tan 30°. About 590 m is the radius for a 60° bank, not 30°.

questions.q: In a steady, power-off glide, what sets the glide angle?
options: The weight alone: heavier aircraft glide more steeply
questions.why: With T = 0, resolving gives D = W sin γ and L = W cos γ, so tan γ = D/L. Weight affects the speed of the best glide but not its angle, because L/D at a given CL is independent of weight. Wing area likewise changes the speed, not the angle. There is no thrust in a power-off glide.

questions.q: An aircraft of mass 10 000 kg climbs steadily at 80 m/s with thrust 30 kN and drag 18 kN. Find the climb angle and rate of climb, and explain why the lift is slightly less than the weight.
markScheme: RC = V sin γ ≈ 9.8 m/s
Normal to path: L = W cos γ < W
Part of the weight is balanced by thrust along the path
questions.modelAnswer: W = 10 000 × 9.81 = 98 100 N. Along the path, T − D = W sin γ, so sin γ = 12 000/98 100 ≈ 0.122 and γ ≈ 7.0°. Rate of climb RC = V sin γ = 80 × 0.122 ≈ 9.8 m/s. Perpendicular to the path, L = W cos γ ≈ 0.993W. The lift is slightly less than the weight because the flight path is tilted upwards; the component of weight along the path is carried by the excess thrust, so lift only has to balance the component normal to the path.

questions.q: For a jet aircraft modelled with constant TSFC, at which speed is endurance (time aloft) greatest?
questions.why: A jet's fuel flow is TSFC × thrust, so minimum fuel flow means minimum thrust, which is minimum drag at V_md (maximum L/D). The minimum power speed maximises endurance for a propeller aircraft, whose fuel flow scales with power. About 1.32 V_md maximises jet range, not endurance. At the stall speed drag is well above its minimum, so endurance is poorer.

questions.q: A jet cruises at V = 230 m/s with L/D = 17 and TSFC = 0.6 per hour, burning fuel until W₀/W₁ = 1.25. What is the Breguet range?
questions.why: c = 0.6/3600 = 1.667 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, so R = (230/1.667 × 10⁻⁴) × 17 × ln 1.25 ≈ 5.23 × 10⁶ m ≈ 5200 km. About 1.5 km comes from leaving c as 0.6 per hour while V is in metres per second, which mixes time units. About 29 300 km uses W₀/W₁ = 1.25 directly instead of its natural log (0.223). About 4700 km uses the fuel fraction 0.2 in place of ln 1.25; the two are close but not equal, because the logarithm accounts for the aircraft getting lighter as it burns fuel.

questions.q: A transport aircraft has mass 60 000 kg and wing area 120 m². Find its sea-level stall speed (a) clean with CLmax = 1.5 and (b) with flaps giving CLmax = 2.4. Find (c) the stall speed with flaps in a 60° banked level turn.
questions.modelAnswer: W = 60 000 × 9.81 = 588 600 N. (a) V_s = √(2 × 588 600/(1.225 × 120 × 1.5)) = √5339 ≈ 73.1 m/s. (b) With CLmax = 2.4, V_s = √(2 × 588 600/(1.225 × 120 × 2.4)) = √3337 ≈ 57.8 m/s. (c) In a 60° level turn n = 1/cos 60° = 2, so the wing must produce twice the weight in lift. The stall speed scales with √n, giving 57.8 × √2 ≈ 81.7 m/s.

questions.q: According to momentum theory, how does ideal hover power change if the rotor radius is doubled at the same thrust and density?
questions.why: P = T^(3/2)/√(2ρA) and A ∝ R², so P ∝ 1/R. Doubling R halves the power. A quarter would follow if P were proportional to 1/A rather than 1/√A. The power cannot be unchanged because disc loading falls. Doubling would mean power rose with rotor size, which is the opposite of the theory.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the tail rotor on a conventional single-main-rotor helicopter?
options: To increase main rotor lift in hover
To counteract the torque reaction from driving the main rotor
To provide most of the forward thrust
questions.why: Driving the main rotor applies an equal and opposite torque to the fuselage, which the tail rotor's sideways thrust balances; it also gives yaw control. Forward thrust comes from tilting the main rotor with cyclic. Retreating-blade stall is a forward-flight main-rotor limit that the tail rotor cannot fix. The tail rotor actually absorbs some power rather than adding main-rotor lift.

questions.q: Using actuator disc theory, derive the induced velocity in hover and calculate it, together with the ideal power, for a 5000 kg helicopter with a 7.5 m radius rotor at sea level.
markScheme: Mass flow ṁ = ρAvᵢ; far-wake velocity 2vᵢ (from energy/momentum)
T = ṁ × 2vᵢ = 2ρAvᵢ², so vᵢ = √(T/(2ρA))
vᵢ ≈ 10.6 m/s
P = Tvᵢ ≈ 522 kW
questions.modelAnswer: Treat the rotor as an actuator disc of area A. Air starts at rest far above, crosses the disc at vᵢ and reaches w in the far wake. The mass flow is ṁ = ρAvᵢ and the thrust is T = ṁw. The power is the rate of kinetic energy increase, ½ṁw², and it must also equal Tvᵢ = ṁwvᵢ, so w = 2vᵢ. Then T = 2ρAvᵢ² and vᵢ = √(T/(2ρA)). For m = 5000 kg, T = 49 050 N and A = π × 7.5² = 176.7 m². So vᵢ = √(49 050/(2 × 1.225 × 176.7)) ≈ 10.6 m/s, and ideal power P = Tvᵢ ≈ 49 050 × 10.64 ≈ 522 kW.

questions.q: An aircraft's neutral point is at 0.45c̄ and its CG at 0.30c̄. If the lift-curve slope is 5.0 per radian, what is Cm_α?
questions.why: Kₙ = 0.45 − 0.30 = 0.15, and Cm_α = −aKₙ = −5.0 × 0.15 = −0.75 per rad. A positive value has the wrong sign: a CG ahead of the neutral point gives a stable (negative) slope. −0.15 is dCm/dCL (the static margin with sign), not Cm_α. −2.25 uses the neutral point position 0.45 instead of the margin.

questions.q: Which change makes an aircraft more statically stable in pitch?
options: Moving the tailplane closer to the wing
Moving the centre of gravity forward
Moving the centre of gravity aft of the neutral point
questions.why: Moving the CG forward increases the static margin h_n − h, so Cm_α becomes more negative. A CG behind the neutral point makes the aircraft unstable. Reducing the tail area or tail arm lowers the tail volume coefficient, which moves the neutral point forward and reduces stability.

questions.q: Explain why a conventional aircraft needs both Cm_α < 0 and Cm₀ > 0, and why a wing on its own with positive camber cannot usually satisfy both. How does a tailplane help?
markScheme: Cm_α < 0: disturbance in α creates a restoring moment (static stability)
Cm₀ > 0: needed so Cm = 0 occurs at positive α/CL (trim with useful lift)
Positively cambered wing has Cm₀ (about the aerodynamic centre) negative, nose-down
Tail behind CG gives a nose-up moment at zero lift if set at negative incidence (raising Cm₀)
Tail lift rises with α behind the CG, making Cm_α more negative
questions.modelAnswer: With Cm = Cm₀ + Cm_α α, a negative Cm_α means that if a gust raises α, a nose-down moment results, which is static stability. Trim requires Cm = 0, which happens at α = −Cm₀/Cm_α; for this to be a positive angle (positive lift) with Cm_α negative, Cm₀ must be positive. A positively cambered wing has a negative (nose-down) pitching moment at zero lift, so on its own with its CG ahead of the aerodynamic centre it would be stable but would trim only at negative lift. A tailplane mounted behind the CG at a small negative incidence produces a download at zero wing lift, giving a nose-up moment and making Cm₀ positive. As α increases, the tail's lift increases and, acting behind the CG, adds a nose-down moment, making Cm_α more negative.

questions.q: A twin-engine jet transport has mass 60 000 kg, wing area 120 m², aspect ratio 9, Oswald efficiency 0.8 and CD₀ = 0.020. It cruises at 10 km in the ISA (ρ = 0.4127 kg/m³). Take g = 9.81 m/s². (a) Find K, the lift coefficient at maximum L/D and (L/D)max. [4] (b) Find the minimum-drag speed at 10 km and the drag there. [4] (c) The aircraft actually cruises at 230 m/s. Find CL, CD, L/D and the thrust required. [5] (d) Using the Breguet equation with TSFC 0.6 per hour, estimate the range if 20% of the initial weight is burnt as fuel at this cruise condition. [4] (e) Explain why jet aircraft generally cruise faster than the minimum-drag speed. [3]
markScheme: (b) V_md = √(2W/(ρSCL*)) ≈ 188 m/s; D_min = W/(L/D)max ≈ 35.0 kN
(e) Jet range is maximised at max √CL/CD, about 1.32V_md; small drag penalty, larger speed gain; also V_md is on edge of speed stability
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) K = 1/(πeAR) = 1/(π × 0.8 × 9) ≈ 0.0442.
CL at (L/D)max: CL* = √(CD₀/K) = √(0.020/0.0442) ≈ 0.673.
(L/D)max = 1/(2√(KCD₀)) = 1/(2√(0.000884)) ≈ 16.8.

(b) W = 60 000 × 9.81 = 588 600 N.
V_md = √(2W/(ρSCL*)) = √(2 × 588 600/(0.4127 × 120 × 0.673)) ≈ 188 m/s.
D_min = W/(L/D)max = 588 600/16.8 ≈ 35.0 kN.

(c) q = ½ × 0.4127 × 230² ≈ 10 916 Pa.
CL = W/(qS) = 588 600/(10 916 × 120) ≈ 0.449.
CD = 0.020 + 0.0442 × 0.449² ≈ 0.020 + 0.0089 = 0.0289.
L/D = 0.449/0.0289 ≈ 15.5.
Thrust required T = D = W/(L/D) ≈ 588 600/15.53 ≈ 37.9 kN (about 19 kN per engine).

(d) Burning 20% of the initial weight gives W₁ = 0.8W₀, so W₀/W₁ = 1.25 and ln 1.25 ≈ 0.223.
c = 0.6/3600 ≈ 1.667 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹.
R = (V/c)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁) = (230/1.667 × 10⁻⁴) × 15.53 × 0.223 ≈ 4.78 × 10⁶ m, about 4800 km.
(This assumes constant V, L/D and TSFC, which in practice requires a slow cruise-climb as the aircraft gets lighter.)

(e) For a jet with constant TSFC, fuel used per unit distance is proportional to D/V, so the best range is at the speed that minimises D/V, which is maximum √CL/CD at about 3^(1/4)V_md ≈ 1.32V_md (about 247 m/s here). Near V_md the drag curve is flat, so flying faster costs little extra drag but saves a lot of time. Flying at or below V_md would also place the aircraft on the edge of the speed-unstable region of the drag curve. Operators also value time (crew, utilisation), which pushes cruise speed higher still, limited by transonic drag rise.

questions.q: A helicopter of mass 5000 kg has a single main rotor of radius 7.5 m. (a) Using actuator disc theory, derive expressions for the induced velocity and ideal power in hover, stating the assumptions. [7] (b) Calculate the induced velocity, disc loading and ideal power at sea level, and the actual power if the figure of merit is 0.75. [5] (c) Repeat the ideal power calculation at 2000 m in the ISA (ρ = 1.007 kg/m³) and comment. [4] (d) Explain two effects that limit the helicopter's maximum forward speed. [4]
markScheme: (a) Assumptions: steady, incompressible, inviscid, uniform flow through a thin disc; no swirl; air at rest far upstream
(a) Momentum: T = ṁw; energy: P = ½ṁw² = Tvᵢ gives w = 2vᵢ; T = 2ρAvᵢ²; vᵢ = √(T/(2ρA)); P = T^(3/2)/√(2ρA)
(b) T = 49 050 N; A = 176.7 m²; disc loading ≈ 278 N/m²
(b) vᵢ ≈ 10.6 m/s; P_ideal ≈ 522 kW; P_actual ≈ 696 kW
(c) P ∝ 1/√ρ: P_ideal ≈ 576 kW at 2000 m (about 10% more)
(c) Comment: available engine power usually falls with altitude, so hover ceiling is limited
(d) Retreating-blade stall and advancing-tip compressibility (also reverse flow region)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Model the rotor as a thin actuator disc of area A = πR². Assume steady, incompressible, inviscid flow, uniform across the disc, no swirl, and air at rest far above. Let vᵢ be the velocity through the disc and w the velocity in the far wake.
Mass flow: ṁ = ρAvᵢ.
Momentum: the air gains velocity w, so T = ṁw.
Energy: power into the air is P = ½ṁw². The power is also the thrust times the velocity at the disc, P = Tvᵢ = ṁwvᵢ. Equating, w = 2vᵢ.
So T = 2ρAvᵢ², giving vᵢ = √(T/(2ρA)), and the ideal induced power is P = Tvᵢ = T^(3/2)/√(2ρA).

(b) T = 5000 × 9.81 = 49 050 N. A = π × 7.5² ≈ 176.7 m², so disc loading T/A ≈ 278 N/m².
vᵢ = √(49 050/(2 × 1.225 × 176.7)) = √113.3 ≈ 10.6 m/s.
P_ideal = 49 050 × 10.64 ≈ 522 kW.
P_actual = P_ideal/FM = 522/0.75 ≈ 696 kW.

(c) At 2000 m, vᵢ = √(49 050/(2 × 1.007 × 176.7)) ≈ 11.7 m/s and P_ideal ≈ 49 050 × 11.74 ≈ 576 kW. This is √(1.225/1.007) ≈ 1.10 times the sea-level value, about 10% more. At the same time the engine's available power usually falls with altitude, so the margin for hover shrinks; this sets the hover ceiling, and the problem is worse on hot days (higher density altitude).

(d) In forward flight the advancing blade tip sees ΩR + V and the retreating tip ΩR − V. To keep the rolling moment balanced, the retreating blade must work at a higher angle of attack; as forward speed rises it reaches stall (retreating-blade stall), causing vibration and loss of control. Meanwhile the advancing tip approaches the speed of sound, so compressibility effects (shock waves, drag rise and noise) appear. A reverse-flow region also grows near the root of the retreating blade. Together these limit conventional helicopters to modest top speeds compared with fixed-wing aircraft.
